ALiBi (used in MPT-7B, BLOOM) is empirically the most graceful extrapolator for raw perplexity — its linear bias penalty is unbounded and never aliases — but Su et al.'s YaRN work (2023) and the LongBench evaluations both show that ALiBi models suffer a different instruction-following failure: the aggressive distance penalty causes the model to effectively ignore tokens beyond ~2× training length, so a system prompt placed at position 0 becomes geometrically de-weighted relative to recent context, inverting the intended authority hierarchy. The mechanistic crux is that instruction-tuned behavioral constraints are implemented as long-range attention patterns — the refusal circuit, for instance, requires heads in mid-to-late layers to maintain strong attention from the response prefix back to the instruction header — and any encoding scheme that disrupts long-range attention fidelity selectively amputates these circuits while leaving local fluency intact. RoPE's aliasing therefore wins the prize for "steepest instruction-following cliff" because it doesn't just weaken long-range attention — it actively scrambles it into spurious patterns, potentially activating attention heads in ways that mimic attended-but-misaligned instruction signals.

The crossover point between "redundancy helps" and "redundancy interferes" appears to correlate with whether the repetition density causes the system prompt to be processed as episodic content (something that happened in the conversation) versus standing instruction (a persistent behavioral prior), a distinction the model has no explicit architectural mechanism to maintain and must infer purely from positional and semantic context. This reveals that the refusal gate is not a robust logical circuit but a probabilistic attractor whose basin of attraction can be reshaped by manipulating the statistical structure of the context — redundancy is a tool that works until it becomes a signal, at which point it actively undermines the behavior it was meant to preserve.
